youtube.baslik: Case: One-Sided Conductive Loss with a Flat Tympanogram | Lesson 272 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
We work through a fictional adult case of one-sided conductive hearing loss step by step: otoscopy, masked bone conduction and the plateau, speech tests, interpreting ear canal volume with a type B tympanogram, the acoustic reflex pattern, ENT referral and sample report wording.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology; Gelfand, Essentials of Audiology; Jerger, Clinical experience with impedance audiometry (1970); BSA, Recommended Procedure: Pure-tone Air-conduction and Bone-conduction Threshold Audiometry with and without Masking.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: Type B tympanogram and ear canal volume
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we work through our first adult case step by step: conductive loss in one ear and a type B tympanogram.
Together we will apply otoscopy, masked bone conduction, ear canal volume and the audiologist's referral and reporting steps.

maddeler.metin: Own voice echoes on the right

cumleler: Our case is entirely fictional; a thirty-four-year-old adult comes in with reduced hearing in the right ear.
The complaint began about three weeks ago with a feeling of fullness and blockage in the ear.
The history includes a cold shortly before the onset.
There is no ear pain, discharge, tinnitus or dizziness; there is no ear surgery or noise exposure either.
The person says their own voice sounds echoey in the right ear, a sensation often described with conductive problems.
The history points us in a direction, but decisions are always based on all the findings together.
We always start testing with otoscopy; the left ear canal and tympanic membrane look normal.
In the right ear the canal is clear; there is no impacted earwax.
Behind the tympanic membrane there is a yellowish, amber appearance.
A thin air-fluid line and a few bubbles can be seen in the upper part of the drum; the light reflex is not clear.
This appearance suggests fluid in the middle ear, but otoscopy too is interpreted together with the tests, not alone.
In the report we describe what we see only as an appearance, without making a diagnosis.
On pure-tone audiometry, right air conduction thresholds are between 30 and 40 dB HL; testing uses supra-aural earphones.
Left air conduction thresholds are within normal limits.
Right unmasked bone conduction thresholds are in the normal range, between 5 and 10 dB HL.
So there is an air-bone gap of 20 to 30 dB in the right ear.
First the air conduction rule: the difference between right air conduction and the left ear is at most 30 dB, below forty.
So the right air conduction thresholds do not need masking; but bone conduction is a different story.
For bone conduction, interaural attenuation is taken as about zero; an unmasked response may come from the better of the two cochleas.
Because the air-bone gap is 15 dB or more, right bone conduction is measured again with noise in the left ear.
For example, at 1000 hertz the left air conduction threshold is 5 dB HL; initial masking is 10 dB above that.
Because the supra-aural earphone covers the left ear, a 10 dB occlusion correction is added at 1000 hertz; initial masking is 25 dB EM.
As the noise is raised step by step, the right bone conduction threshold stays at 10 dB HL; in other words, there is a plateau.
This plateau value is the true bone conduction threshold of the right cochlea and is recorded with the masked symbol.
After masking, right bone conduction thresholds are between 10 and 15 dB HL; we mark them with square brackets.
The thresholds stayed very close to the unmasked values, so the bone conduction responses really come from the right cochlea.
The left ear is within normal limits at all frequencies.
The right ear has an air-bone gap of about 15 to 30 dB, confirmed with masking.
The pure-tone average, the mean of 500, 1000 and 2000 hertz, is 35 dB HL; this is a mild degree.
The picture is consistent with a mild conductive hearing loss in the right ear.

maddeler.metin: Weber _to the right_, Rinne negative right

cumleler: The right speech reception threshold, or SRT, is 35 dB HL; it matches the pure-tone average exactly.
The right word recognition score is 96 percent; in conductive loss, understanding is usually good once sound is loud enough.
Because the word test was given at 75 dB HL, the left ear was masked to prevent crossover to the opposite ear.
In the left ear, the SRT is 10 dB HL and the word recognition score is 100 percent.
On the tuning fork Weber test, sound lateralizes to the right, the problem ear; the Rinne test is negative on the right.
The tuning fork findings point the same way as the audiogram; tests confirming each other is the cross-check principle.
Now to the immittance findings; the left ear has a type A tympanogram with a normal-height peak near zero pressure.
In the right ear the curve is flat; no clear peak forms as pressure changes, in other words a type B tympanogram.
A type B curve has more than one meaning, so the first step is to look at the ear canal volume, or ECV.
The right ECV is one milliliter; the left is similar, at zero point nine milliliters.
In adults, ECV is about zero point six to one point five milliliters, so the right ear volume is in the normal range.
A type B curve with normal volume suggests an intact eardrum with an immobile space behind it.

sahneler.baslik: What does *volume* tell us in type B?
cumleler: If volume is normal for age with a type B curve, the most common possibility is middle ear effusion, meaning fluid in the middle ear.
In our case, otoscopy also shows a fluid appearance behind the drum, so the findings support each other.
If volume is clearly large, for example around three milliliters, the probe tone is passing through an opening into the middle ear.
In that case a perforation or a patent ventilation tube is considered; otoscopy looks for an opening in the drum.
If volume is very small, the probe tip may be against the canal wall, or the canal may be blocked with wax.
So reporting a type B curve without looking at its volume is an incomplete interpretation.
We read the acoustic reflex results by naming them after the ear that receives the stimulus.
With the probe in the right ear, in the right ipsilateral measure, there is no reflex; a fluid-filled middle ear shows no admittance change.
The left contralateral reflex, with the stimulus on the left and the probe on the right, is absent for the same reason.
With the stimulus right and the probe left, the reflex is again absent; the right conductive loss lowers the level reaching the cochlea.
With probe and stimulus both on the left, the reflex is present at 85 dB HL, the expected level.
This is the typical pattern of a one-sided conductive problem: no reflex when the problem ear holds the probe or gets the stimulus.
Otoscopy shows a fluid appearance behind the right eardrum.
The audiogram shows a mild conductive loss on the right, an air-bone gap confirmed with masking and a good speech score.
Immittance shows a right type B tympanogram with normal volume and reflex findings consistent with a one-sided conductive pattern.
Together these findings are consistent with middle ear effusion; this is an interpretation, and the diagnosis is made by the physician.
Because right bone conduction is normal, no inner ear problem appears on these tests.
The audiologist's first step is to refer the person, with the findings, to an ear, nose and throat, or ENT, physician.
The referral note includes the otoscopic appearance, the audiogram, tympanogram and ECV values, and the reflex findings.
In an adult, a one-sided effusion that does not clear may require the physician to investigate its cause further.
So the duration and one-sidedness are stated clearly in the note; decisions such as examining the nasopharynx belong to the physician.
The physician decides on treatment; the audiologist recommends no medication or procedure and only explains why follow-up testing matters.
After the physician's assessment, a follow-up audiogram and tympanogram document the recovery.

sahneler.metin: With a type B curve, check the volume first, then compare with otoscopy. If they disagree, reseat the probe.
cumleler: A clinical tip: when you see a flat curve, check the volume before interpreting it.
If the volume is very small, check the probe tip, and if needed measure again with a better-fitting tip and the right angle.
Then compare with your otoscopy; a fluid appearance on otoscopy and a type B curve with normal volume support each other.
If the findings disagree, repeating the measurement is always better than writing a wrong referral note.

maddeler.metin: Comment: may be consistent with effusion

cumleler: In a sample report, the pure-tone result could read: mild conductive hearing loss in the right ear, left ear within normal limits.
Immittance section: right type B tympanogram, ear canal volume one milliliter; left type A tympanogram.
Reflex section: reflexes absent with the probe in the right ear and with right stimulation; left ipsilateral reflex at the expected level.
Comment: findings may be consistent with right middle ear fluid; bone conduction is within normal limits in both ears.
Recommendation: ENT assessment, and a follow-up audiogram and tympanometry at the time the physician recommends.
The report also states the type of earphone used and the masking levels.
Let us look at a sample follow-up test done a few weeks after the physician's assessment.
The dashed red line shows the first right air conduction thresholds, and the green line the thresholds at follow-up.
Right air conduction thresholds are back between 10 and 20 dB HL; bone conduction is at the same level.
At 1000 hertz there is a 25 dB improvement; the air-bone gap has closed.
The tympanogram is now type A, and reflexes are present with the probe in the right ear.
Had there been no improvement, this would also have been reported to the physician just as clearly.

maddeler.metin: Otoscopy first, then masked bone conduction
Type B volume: fluid, hole or blockage
Report with values, plan a retest

cumleler: To confirm a conductive loss, the air-bone gap is measured with masked bone conduction.
With a type B tympanogram, ear canal volume guides interpretation: normal suggests fluid, large an opening, small a blockage.
Otoscopy, audiogram and immittance are interpreted together; diagnosis and treatment decisions belong to the physician.
The report includes measured values, the person is referred to an ENT physician and a follow-up test is planned.

sahneler.soru: Right type B, ECV 3.2 mL. What is considered?
sahneler.aciklama: Volume is very large: the probe tone reaches the middle ear _through an opening in the drum_.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: an adult has a right type B tympanogram with an ear canal volume of 3.2 milliliters. What is considered?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: a perforation or a patent ventilation tube.
The volume is well above the adult range; the probe tone is also measuring the middle ear space through an opening in the drum.
